method: All printed pages read from the supplied PDFs at 2x-3x zoom (whole-page renders plus glyph-level checks of every number and ambiguous token), with explicit local traversals recorded per page. Ordered source blocks include every instructional bullet, table row/cell, flowchart step, diagram label, arrow annotation, legend entry and caption. Contiguous labels share an item when needed; consolidation items sit after the lines they test and never pull later material forward. Headers, timestamps, footers and blank Active space excluded.
caveats: Ch9 p753-755: auto-generated source checklist from existing 52 questions, each mapped to its printed line in book order. Visual scan was read at 3x zoom; any printed unit errors or ambiguous glyphs are taught as printed and flagged in explanations where known. No new medical facts introduced beyond the scan.

elements.source: The listed causes of thrombotic microangiopathy are HUS, HELLP syndrome, malignant hypertension and the rheumatological conditions: [Causes: HUS; HELLP; rheumatological condition – catastrophic APS, diffuse scleroderma; malignant hypertension. (Book p753)]
The expansion of HELLP syndrome as written is: [HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzyme, low platelet). (Book p753)]

Match each condition with its renal-vessel category — 1) Catastrophic APS / diffuse scleroderma 2) Takayasu arteritis / polyarteritis nodosa 3) Malignant hypertension … A) Accelerated HTN + papilloedema B) Smaller vessels of kidney C) Larger vessels of kidney [Catastrophic APS/diffuse scleroderma involve smaller vessels of kidney v/s larger vessels (Takayasu, PAN); malignant HTN = accelerated HTN + papilloed]
The antibody annotated with diffuse scleroderma in the cause list is: [Diffuse scleroderma (anti RNA P). (Book p753)]
Malignant hypertension is defined in the book as accelerated HTN plus: [Malignant hypertension = accelerated HTN + papilloedema. (Book p753)]
Emergency hypertension in the malignant-HTN note is end-organ damage with a BP of at least: [Emergency HTN: end organ damage + ≥180/120; new onset fundal changes: hemorrhage/exudate. (Book p753)]

Fill up: In the malignant-hypertension note, the new onset fundal changes are written as hemorrhage/______. [The bracket reads: (New onset fundal changes: hemorrhage/exudate + emergency HTN: end organ damage + ≥180/120). (Book p753)]

The heading 'Rheumatological Condition' is bracketed against catastrophic APS and diffuse scleroderma, and not against HUS or HELLP. [The causes list runs HUS, HELLP, then the rheumatological bracket over catastrophic APS and diffuse scleroderma (Anti RNA P), then malignant hypertens]
Fill up: The HUS triad is thrombocytopenia, renal failure and ______. [Triad: thrombocytopenia, renal failure, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA). (Book p753)]
All of the following form the HUS triad EXCEPT: [Fever belongs to the TTP pentad, not the HUS triad. (Book p753)]
Compared with the HUS triad, the TTP pentad adds fever, GI symptoms and: [TTP pentad: thrombocytopenia, fever, MAHA, neurological symptoms [brain], GI symptoms. (Book p753)]
Which statement comparing the two shapes is TRUE? [Triad vs pentagon as drawn: TTP adds GI symptoms, fever and neurological symptoms [brain]. (Book p753)]
Typical HUS/D+ begins in childhood, commonly below the age of: [Typical HUS/D+ onset: childhood, commonly age <5 years; cause: infection i.e dysentery; prognosis good. (Book p753)]
Atypical HUS/D- differs from typical HUS by: [Atypical HUS/D-: any age; genetic (m/c)/sporadic (drug induced); bad prognosis (50% progress to ESRD); ↑ recurrence after renal transplant. (Book p753]

Every corner of the TTP pentagon is listed below EXCEPT: [The pentagon carries thrombocytopenia, fever, MAHA, neurological symptoms (brain) and GI symptoms; renal failure is the third corner of the HUS triang]

What is written in square brackets beneath 'Neurological symptoms' in the TTP pentagon? [The pentagon's vertex is labelled 'Neurological Symptoms [Brain]', localising the fifth feature of the TTP pentad. (Book p753)]

In the TYPES table, what proportion of atypical HUS cases progress to ESRD? [The prognosis row for atypical HUS/D− prints 'Bad (50% progress to ESRD)' along with increased chances of recurrence after renal transplant, while typ]

A 34-year-old with dysentery-negative HUS is counselled before a living-related transplant. Which line of the TYPES table applies to him? [The atypical column lists any-age onset, genetic (m/c) or sporadic drug-induced cause, bad prognosis with 50% progress to ESRD and increased chances o]

elements.source: The pathophysiology chain starts with endothelial damage, which next causes: [Endothelial damage → VWF release → platelet plug formation. (Book p754)]
Fill up: In the TMA flowchart, platelets trapped in the plug produce ______. [Platelet trapped in plug → thrombocytopenia. (Book p754)]
Schistocyte formation and hence MAHA arise because: [Schistocyte formation d/t platelet plug circulating erythrocytes damage → MAHA. (Book p754)]
Typical/childhood HUS accounts for what proportion of cases? [Typical/childhood: 90% cases, toxin driven. (Book p754)]

Match each toxin with its organism — 1) Shiga like toxin / verocytotoxin 2) Shiga toxin 3) Neuraminidase toxin … A) Shigella dysentery B) Streptococcus pneumoniae C) Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (O157:H7) [Shiga like toxin/verocytotoxin – EHEC O157:H7; Shiga toxin – Shigella dysentery; neuraminidase toxin – Streptococcus pneumoniae. (Book p754)]
The enterohemorrhagic E. coli strain flagged as m/c is: [EHEC O157:H7 (m/c). (Book p754)]

In the pathophysiology flowchart, thrombocytopenia is reached by which route? [The diagram drops a branch from platelet plug formation: 'Platelet trapped in plug → Thrombocytopenia', running parallel to the schistocyte/MAHA limb.]
Genetic (atypical) HUS is caused by activation of the alternate complement pathway, with the complement profile: [A/w: low C3, normal C4. (Book p754)]

Match each genetic type of atypical HUS with its prognostic label — 1) Complement factor-H mutation 2) Complement factor-B 3) Membrane cofactor-P (MCP) … A) Worst prognosis B) Best prognosis C) m/c mutation [Factor-H (m/c) mutation; factor-B worst prognosis; MCP best prognosis; factor-I also listed. (Book p754)]
Among sporadic drug-induced HUS agents, the pair also bracketed to TTP is: [Ticlopidine + clopidogrel are annotated "TTP also" among drug-induced causes. (Book p754)]

The immune-mediated HUS list contains quinine, gemcitabine, quetiapine and cotrimoxazole; the odd one out from that list is: [Mitomycin sits under sporadic drug-induced causes, not immune-mediated HUS. (Book p754)]
On the peripheral blood smear, schistocytes become significant beyond: [Peripheral blood smear: schistocyte (>2% significant). (Book p754)]
The hemolysis work-up in HUS shows: [Blood investigation: ↑ LDH, −ve Coombs test, ↑ indirect bilirubin, ↓ haptoglobin level, normal PT/APTT. (Book p754)]

Match each column with its complement signature — 1) Atypical HUS pathway 2) SLE pathway 3) Atypical HUS C4 … A) Classical B) Alternative C) Normal [Atypical HUS: alternative pathway, low C3 (N) C4; SLE: classical pathway, low C3 low C4. (Book p754)]

In the coagulation line of the blood investigation block, what is stated as normal? [The blood-investigation list runs: ↑LDH, -ve Coombs test, ↑indirect bilirubin, ↓haptoglobin level, Normal - PT/APTT — normal clotting helps distinguis]

Match each sporadic drug-induced agent with the position of its listing — 1) Tacrolimus and cyclosporine 2) Ticlopidine and clopidogrel 3) Mitomycin … A) Grouped under calcineurin inhibitors B) Marked 'TTP also' C) The first bullet of the drug list D) Listed under immune-mediated HUS only [The sporadic block lists mitomycin first, then gemcitabine and bevacizumab, then 'Calcineurin inhibitors: tacrolimus, cyclosporine', then ticlopidine ]

Gemcitabine appears twice in the causes diagram — once as a sporadic drug-induced agent and once under immune-mediated HUS. [Gemcitabine is the second bullet of 'Sporadic: Drug induced' and the second bullet of 'Immune mediated HUS' on the same page. (Book p754)]

All of the following are printed under the sporadic drug-induced column EXCEPT: [The drug column lists mitomycin, gemcitabine, bevacizumab, calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine), ticlopidine, clopidogrel and cisplatin; ]

elements.source: The typical HUS timeline runs: abdominal pain, then 2 days later bloody dysentery (evaluate & start antibiotics), and after 5 more days: [Abdominal pain → 2 days → bloody dysentery → 5 days → 90-95% resolution; 5-10% HUS. (Book p755)]
After the dysentery phase, the proportion that goes on to HUS is: [90-95% resolution; 5-10% HUS. (Book p755)]
The treatment written for typical HUS is: [Typical HUS treatment: conservative (evaluate & start antibiotics for the dysentery). (Book p755)]
Atypical HUS presents with thrombocytopenia plus features of: [Atypical HUS: features of 2° HTN (renal/endocrine); thrombocytopenia. (Book p755)]
The mainstay of atypical HUS treatment, to be started within 24 hours, is: [PLEX (plasma exchange therapy): within 24 hr; mainstay of treatment. (Book p755)]

In atypical HUS, the costly terminal-complement drug and the immunosuppressant indication written for complement factor H mutation are: [Eculizumab: costly; immunosuppressant in complement factor H mutation; renal transplant listed. (Book p755)]
Recurrence of HUS after renal transplant is managed with: [Recurrence post transplant: rituximab; eculizumab. (Book p755)]

Match each feature with its column in the pre-renal vs ATN note — 1) Urine output in pre-renal injury 2) BUN/creatinine in ATN 3) Tubular injury in pre-renal injury … A) < 10:1 B) Normal C) Absent (−) [Pre-renal: normal urine output, − edema, − tubular injury; ATN: decreased output, <10:1 BUN/Cr, + tubular injury. (Book p755)]
The two BUN ratios written side by side in the note table are: [BUN/creatinine: >20:1 pre-renal; <10:1 ATN. (Book p755)]
Which statement from the pre-renal vs ATN table is TRUE? [Pre-renal: fluids given, edema −, tubular injury −; ATN: fluids withhold, edema +, tubular injury +. (Book p755)]

Fill up: In the typical HUS timeline, the bloody dysentery stage carries the instruction 'Evaluate & ______'. [The flow reads: Abdominal pain → 2 days → Bloody dysentery (Evaluate & start antibiotics) → 5 days → 90–95% Resolution or 5–10% HUS. (Book p755)]

How long after the onset of bloody dysentery does the timeline allow before the child resolves or develops HUS? [Two intervals are printed: 2 days from abdominal pain to bloody dysentery, then 5 days from dysentery to the 90–95% resolution versus 5–10% HUS split.]

Each of these is a listed treatment line for atypical HUS EXCEPT: [The atypical list runs PLEX (within 24hr; mainstay of treatment), eculizumab (costly), immunosuppressant in complement factor H mutation, renal transp]

In the note table, eculizumab is printed twice — once as a treatment line and once under 'Recurrence post transplant'. [Eculizumab is the second treatment bullet ('Costly') and reappears beneath 'Recurrence post transplant' with rituximab. (Book p755)]

Match each row of the note table with what is printed for acute tubular necrosis — 1) Urine output 2) Edema 3) BUN/Creatinine … A) > 20:1 B) Decreased C) + D) − [The necrosis column reads: urine output decreased, edema +, BUN/creatinine < 10:1, fluids withhold, tubular injury +; the pre-renal column reverses ed]

Fill up: The second column of the note table is headed acute tubular ______, exactly as printed. [The table headers are 'Pre renal injury' and 'Acute tubular necrosis' — this page uses necrosis, whereas p749 expands ATN as acute tubular nephrosis. ]
